title: Google Research shows a phone photo can approximate a DXA scan for metabolic risk
subtitle: PhotoScan, trained on 35,000 UK Biobank participants and validated against clinical DXA, estimates body fat distribution well enough to improve insulin-resistance classification from images alone.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: On August 17, Google Research published 'Seeing beyond BMI: Estimating cardiometabolic risk with smartphone imagery,' introducing PhotoScan — a deep-learning method that estimates body composition from ordinary phone photos. The team pretrained the model on 35,323 UK Biobank participants and fine-tuned it on a diverse clinical cohort of 677 people with DXA ground truth. Against the reference scan, PhotoScan hit a mean absolute error of 2.15 percent for total body fat, 0.11 for the Android-to-Gynoid fat ratio, and 0.09 for the visceral-to-subcutaneous fat ratio. The corresponding paper is on arXiv.

The clinical claim is the important one. BMI has been the field's default cardiometabolic screen for decades and it is a poor one — it cannot distinguish visceral from subcutaneous fat, which is where much of the actual insulin-resistance signal lives. Adding PhotoScan's image-derived body-composition metrics to a baseline of age, sex and ethnicity produced insulin-resistance classification performance nearly equivalent to adding clinical-grade DXA data. In practical terms, a two-photo capture on a phone got the model most of the way to a scan that costs hundreds of dollars and requires a hospital visit.

This is part of a broader move by Google, Apple and Amazon-backed health labs to push metabolic screening out of the clinic and into consumer hardware. Apple's cardio work, Google's earlier retinal imaging model for cardiovascular risk, and the recent wave of continuous-glucose consumer devices are all aimed at the same thing: catching risk earlier and cheaper than a specialist appointment can. PhotoScan is notable because it uses no special sensor — just a smartphone camera — which is what determines whether a tool actually reaches primary care in low-resource settings.

A takeaway for learners: the interesting AI-in-medicine work is not always about replacing the specialist. It is often about approximating an expensive gold-standard measurement well enough that screening becomes possible where it currently is not. If you are studying machine learning and you want work that clearly matters, look for problems where the gold-standard exists but is inaccessible. Getting to 90 percent of a DXA scan on a phone is more useful, at population scale, than getting to 100 percent in a lab that most patients never enter.
